utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case Number IT-02-60-T, The Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest last night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, please continue your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Maric. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you recall, yesterday at the end of the day, we spoke about the duties, powers, and competence of the duty operations officer. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will put just a few more questions to you about the situation in the duty operations room, and then we will move on and talk about the events of those days. Please tell us where were duty officers' duties performed physically?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the office of the duty officer in the command. It was on the first floor, and it was the first office to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this a separate office used only by the duty operations officer, for that specific purpose?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a separate office designated for the performance of that duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the rules, was entry prohibited to anyone else but the duty operations officer to that office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were not the duty operations officer or his assistant or the courier were not allowed to enter that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us what kind of communications equipment was available to the duty operations officer in that office.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer in that office had an external line, a telephone line, and he had another telephone which had an internal connection within the barracks. And through the switchboard to all the units in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's be quite specific about this. Does this mean that in that office there were two telephones available to the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There were two telephones that the duty operations officer could use.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a Motorola or a UKT piece of equipment or a RUP piece of equipment in that office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This equipment was not there. It was in the communications centre which was one floor above that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was upstairs above the duty operations office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our brigade's communication centre with all this equipment, radio equipment. It was a normal switchboard, both telephone and radio switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's apply this specifically to the situation at the time. You were on duty on the 12th, and you had to call the command of the Drina Corps, Zlatar. How were you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would contact Zlatar by contacting the switchboard. The switchboard would respond, and I would say, "Put Zlatar on the line." I would stay on the line. I would hear them looking for Zlatar, making the connection. Zlatar would respond. Or I would be put through to the switchboard, and I would ask for whoever I wanted. That's how communications were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At your request, did your switchboard call Zlatar's switchboard and ask for a specific person, the one you requested, or did they call the person you were looking for directly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often, I would ask for the Zlatar switchboard. They would put me through to them, and then I would ask for a specific person. That was the most frequent situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you would call your switchboard, your switchboard would put you through to Zlatar's switchboard, and then through Zlatar's switchboard, you would ask for a specific person?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, this is what happened most often. But sometimes I would tell our switchboard, "Find so-and-so at Zlatar," and they would set up communications with that person, and then they would pass it on to me. So both ways could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you assist us now and see what this looked like the other way around. You as the duty operations officer would receive a call from someone from Zlatar or Badem, the Bratunac Brigade. How did that communication function? How was it established? Would they call you directly or would they go through the Zvornik communications centre?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were going through the switchboard, the switchboard would put them through to me, and they would tell me, "You've got Zlatar on the line." I would respond as the duty officer and start the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did it happen in practice that the duty officer from Zlatar or from Badem or from whatever position would tell your operator, "Pass on such and such a message to the duty operations officer," without contacting you directly? Did this kind of situation occur?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this happened sometimes. I might get messages in this manner. Or maybe by radio. All the messages sent by radio would come to the centre, and they would bring me a telegram which I would open and read. I would see who it was from and what it was about. It would also happen that the person calling didn't use this kind of connection. They would call directly through the telephone, public telephone network, because that was a telephone we had. And that's how we would establish contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So both kinds of communication could be used?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Three kinds of communication, because there was also the radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one more thing: When daily and interim combat reports were sent, whose documents were those? Who signed daily and interim combat reports?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are official brigade documents, and the commander of the brigade would know what they contained, and he would sign them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, information for the higher commands, the superior commands, was sent through the daily and interim combat reports. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This was a regular duty performed by the unit. By 2200 hours, the daily report would be sent. And the information it had to contain was well established, and then it was forwarded to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: What was the duty of the duty operations officer in this whole procedure of compiling and dispatching daily and interim combat reports forwarded to the superior commands? What was the role of the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty operations officer, based on the events that had occurred during the day, during his shift, would prepare the report as a draft, and he would take it to the commander for approval. The commander would read it. He might perhaps add something or alter something. And in the end, he would sign it. And then the report would be sent by telegram to the corps command. Let me say that no report or telegram could be sent, the communications centre would not agree to send it unless it was signed by the commander and chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So hypothetically speaking, if the duty operations officer had to send a daily combat report to the superior command at 2200 hours, the encryptor and the signalsman would not send such a report unless it was signed by the brigade commander and chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. Every document sent through the communications centre had to be signed, and especially the report, because this contained not only information as to what had been happening, but also our requests to the superior command or questions concerning our previous requests. It was a very important document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems logical now to ask, was it ever possible for the duty operations officer on his own initiative to send off a daily or interim combat report without the knowledge, approval, and signature of the commander or the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, we have had the opportunity here to see various daily and interim combat reports containing a text, and then the signature of the commander or chief of staff, and then in the margin, the initials of the duty operations officer, slash, most often MV, Misko Vasic as the man on duty in the office. Would you please explain to us the method or rather what these initials mean? Why are they there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the bottom of the report on the left-hand side were first the initials of the person who compiled the report, which was most often the duty operations officer, slash, the person who typed it out. And on the right-hand side would be the commander's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So it was only when it had been signed by the commander or the chief of staff that the encryptor could dispatch this report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That was what happened as far as I know. No document could be sent off if it had not been signed and approved by the commander or the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the commander and the chief were the persons whose duty it was to make sure that the superior command was informed on time of all the events in the area of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The commander had to be informed of everything that had happened, of the entire overall situation in this area of defence. And through this report, he had to inform the superior command of the overall situation so that the superior command would know what the situation was in their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could just tell us how this procedure functioned from the top down to a lower unit. You said that the duty operations officer could never issue orders to battalion commanders, to units within the brigade. Sometimes you would have the situation that the superior command or the commander or the chief of staff would ask its battalion to do something. Can this go through the duty officer; and if so, how is it done? What does the operations duty officer do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subordinate units also had a certain time period, two hours or so, before the brigade compiled its daily report. They had time to send in their report to the duty officer in the brigade. And then there would be a complete report made from those summarised reports for the entire brigade. Sometimes it could happen that the battalion commander would ask the brigade to do something through its daily report or in regular communications with the duty officer, if the commander wasn't there. Maybe he would ask for artillery support or ask for ammunition, food, anything from the command brigade. And this information would reach the duty officer. The duty officer, if the commander or the chief of staff were not there, would know where they were. If the message was urgent and it could not wait for them to return, they would look for him and convey to him that order or would convey the requests for a certain unit, what it is they were requesting. Based on the answer or the response of the commander or the chief of staff, that order would be transferred further. So if the commander said, "Order the artillery chief to fire such and such a number of shells in that sector," this would be written down and conveyed to the person who was supposed to implement that order. This is how this functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since we have these notes in the operations -- duty operations officer notebook, the commander or the chief of staff needs to take a number of soldiers from a battalion and engage them in some other area to protect the lines or to give them a different assignment that they needed to carry out. Can the commander tell this directly to the battalion commander, or can this be conveyed through the duty officer? "I require ten soldiers from the 1st Battalion to go to the Orahovac sector," the commander says. Where is the operations duty officer in all of this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander could communicate directly with his subordinates. He could call the battalion commander directly and issue him an order. And he could also say that to the operations officer and say, "Send such and such a message to such and such a battalion that ten soldiers be sent to such and such a sector." So both of these ways were possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible for the duty operations officer to say on his own to the battalion to send ten soldiers to Orahovac without having such a request or an order from the commander or the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible, and as I said at the beginning, I was a battalion commander. And if I received such a message, it was impossible to receive such a message because the duty operations officer did not have the right to issue such an order. And it would seem like a joke to me. It was just not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want to say that you as battalion commander would never accept something like that from the duty operations officer but would seek an order from the commander or chief of staff? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may put your question another way, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Maric, the question is as follows: Is it possible, then, ever for the commander of the battalion to accept such an order from the duty operations officer without this being backed by an order from the commander or the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. "Is it possible ever ..." That is just so wide open in the context of human existence that it really doesn't help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, during the time you were the battalion commander, as you said, did such a situation ever occur that a duty operations officer would request something without it being backed by the commander or the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not possible for the duty operations officer to issue such an order. He can convey the order from the commander or the chief of staff. But he himself could not order anything to the unit. This is impossible. And if he did, no commander would implement this. They would ask, "Whose orders are these? Could we have a direct communication with the commander or the chief of staff to clarify the order?" And then it could be implemented. That was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question: Is the duty operations officer duty-bound to ask the commander or the chief of staff why he required those soldiers in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the duty operations officer does not have that right, and this did not happen for him to ask for an explanation or clarification of an order. The commander issues orders, but there can be no disobedience or questioning of such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. We will come back to certain notes that you made when we propose to tender documents as exhibits. Now we are going to move to a different topic. On the 12th of July 1995 in the morning, you took over as duty operations officer. Could you please briefly tell us what you did as duty operations officer that day. Were there any characteristic events?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of May [as interpreted] when I took over the duty, I found out that a larger group of Muslims were blocked in the region of the 8th Battalion and that fighting had already started. I received information that one Muslim was captured, that there were four killed. And the commander in the course of the day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Stojanovic. The transcript said the 12th of May. I think it's a mistake. It should be July. Can we correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, I just wanted to clarify something, Mr. Maric. Are you speaking about the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the 12th of July when I was the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I will just use this to interrupt you for a moment. From whom did you receive information about there being one captured and a certain number of killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this information from the 8th Battalion, through our communications centre, and I wrote down this information in the duty operations notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the 8th Battalion? Where was it located? In which sector?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 8th Battalion was located near Bratunac, and its command post was in Kajici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After you received this information, what did you, as duty operations officer, do? Who did you inform?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to regular procedure, I informed the chief of staff. And he immediately ordered me to convey this to Petkovic from the intelligence organ and for him to go to Kajica Potok to get the prisoner. I informed him and conveyed the order to Petkovic to do what the chief of staff ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened later? Did you receive any return information about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not receive any return information about that. I don't know whether he went there or not. And I don't know what happened later.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last sentence of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, the chief dictated an order for me for subordinate units, and this related to the preparation of the units to allocate a certain number of men and to keep them ready in the sectors of their commands, to allocate one platoon each up to about 40 soldiers, to keep it ready in their units except for the 4th and the 7th Battalions which were supposed to take up with one platoon positions in the depth of their defence in order to prevent an attack from the rear. This is the 4th Battalion in Baljkovica and the 5th Battalion in Memici. The 4th Battalion is to occupy an area in Motovska Kosa in the depth of their zone, and the 7th Battalion was supposed to occupy Cetino Brdo and Drenovic. Then he ordered one group--

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, Mr. Maric, I need to interrupt you for a second. Everything has to go into the transcript, everything that you say. So I will ask you once again to speak more slowly if you can. And the last sentence of your previous answer was not recorded. Could you please repeat it. I will ask you again. Did you ever receive any kind of return information about what the intelligence organs did in regard to the captured person in the 8th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not during my shift receive any information. My assistant neither was informed about what happened with the implementation of that order. So we didn't receive any information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, we will go back to what we were talking about. After the commander issued that order to inform the battalions, did you convey that to the battalions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I think that the chief of staff dictated this order, and this order was conveyed to all the battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any troop or unit movements that evening within the zone of defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, the 12th, there were no activities. There were some sporadic mortar fire in the front section, but nothing significant happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Obrenovic that evening move a part of the Kiseljak or 2nd Battalion to new positions that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the telegram, Obrenovic ordered one self-propelled gun and one armoured transporter to be ready, and these other battalions that were supposed to provide the men were to be ready. This included the 2nd or the Kiseljak Battalion. There were no movements outside of the zone. All the units were in their place. After this telegram, the chief -- I saw it out in the corridor when he issued an order to Dusko Vukotic to go with a group of military policemen for reconnaissance in the area of Lijesanj and Dzafin Kamen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they go?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see if they went or not. I just heard it out in the corridor when the chief of staff issued an order that he should go for reconnaissance with a group of military police in order to gather information about this column about which we had received information. We received information about its movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if you received any information or instructions from the Drina Corps or from the Ministry of Defence that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A telegram arrived that day, it looked more like it came from a civilian structure, from the Ministry of Defence rather than from a military structure, to look at the transport options, buses and trucks, in the area of the Drina Corps, to secure buses and other transport for Srebrenica. As soon as I received this telegram, I gave it to the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, what was being requested of the Zvornik Brigade in this telegram in view of securing these buses?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can understand, it was a general telegram for all the municipalities requesting all transport vehicles, trucks, buses, to be sent to Bratunac in order to evacuate the population from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that all of the buses should assemble in Bratunac. Do you remember where they were supposed to assemble in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I remember the telegram, and it looked like a civilian telegram more as a kind of information. Because in the Zvornik Brigade, we didn't have our own buses. I think we had two buses, but they were not in very good working order. We ourselves when we used the buses, when our unit used buses, we relied on the civilian structures, on the passenger transport companies, or through the ministry, we would secure the transport for our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You as duty operations officer, did you have any authority to requisition these vehicles from civilian structures?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As duty operations officer, I did not have any competencies over that segment, the one that you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me phrase this as a question. How would mobilisation or requisitioning procedure be carried out if there was a need, for example, to transport buses of the Zvornik Brigade? What would that procedure look like?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zvornik Brigade sent a lot of its units out on the field. And frequently, we would use buses. As I've said, we did not have those buses within our unit, so the most frequent procedure to secure buses was to have the chief of staff or commander inform the chief of transportation services in the brigade which was Mr. Pantic who used to work in a transportation company before the war. And then he would contact the Ministry of Defence because he knew how many buses there were, he knew whether they were in working order. And then he would contact the Ministry of Defence and ensure that a certain company provide a certain number of buses which would assemble at a certain point, at a certain hour. Therefore, he would also ensure fuel, food for the drivers, and everything else that was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the brigade was not able to take a vehicle from civilian structures directly, would rather have to go through the Ministry of Defence and their office in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally wasn't present at any occasion where somebody from the brigade would go and personally requisition a vehicle. I think that it had to go through the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: By the way, let me ask you, in that system, the chief of arms of service, would he be able to go directly to civilian structures and requisition a vehicle that was needed by the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether he could do that, I don't know. Let me tell you, it was wartime, and according to the rules this was within the scope of authorities of the ministry. Most frequently, somebody from the ministry, somebody from the unit or chief of arms of service would, together with this requisitioning request, supported by the Ministry of Defence go and requisition a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, who would have to sign that request in that system, the request to requisition a vehicle? Could that be the duty operations officer, or would that have to be the chief of arms of service, or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These requests, all of the requests where a stamp was needed, because only a document signed by the commander or chief of staff could be stamped. So that was the required procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. Do you know why those buses were needed on the 12th of July? Why were they requested? Did anybody tell you this? Did you have any other sources of information? Do you know why those buses were needed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think we have spent a lot of time on that issue. And it seems to me that everything is clear. Would you please move forward, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that on the 12th of July, civilians were transported from Potocari towards Tuzla and Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know, a duty operations officer didn't know. I didn't receive any such information that anybody was transported towards our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th, did you see Dragan Jokic anywhere in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think there's some confusion in that. Mr. Stojanovic if he knew of anyone transported towards Kladanj, and the witness said he was not aware of anyone that was transported into the area of Zvornik. So I don't think the question was responsive, but it just may be because of a misunderstanding of the question. Kladanj, of course, as we know is not in the Zvornik area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, maybe you could have it clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, on that day, on the 12th, did you know about the transportation of civilians from Potocari towards Kladanj or Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As duty operations officer, I didn't know about their transportation. I didn't know about transportation of civilian populations from Srebrenica towards Kladanj and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And following that, I asked you whether on the 12th of July, did you see anywhere in the command of Zvornik Brigade Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see Jokic on the 12th while I was on duty as duty operations officer at all, nor do I know where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, as duty operations officer, did you on the 12th know anything about opportunistic killings which took place in Srebrenica, Jadar, Konjevic Polje, and Sandici, and Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have that information. This information did not reach the duty operations officer, or myself personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you spend the night between the 12th and 13th of July? And were you still on duty that night as duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was on duty until the morning on the 13th. I managed to sleep a little bit. My assistant stood in for me. And I was on duty until the morning of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the assistant to the duty operations officer, let me put a few questions to you regarding that. What are the duties of the assistant duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duties of the assistant duty operations officer is to replace him while the duty operations officer is resting. The assistant would normally be an officer who had less knowledge about what was going on and would inform the duty operations officer about anything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, would an assistant normally be an officer or a noncommissioned officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, the assistant would be a noncommissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That night between the 12th and the 13th of July, were there any intense combat operations going on? Were there any problems in the area of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was no combat action going on, nothing of significance was going on in the area of defence of the brigade. There was no movement of units. The self-propelled vehicle and Praga were standing ready. Those were the orders, the orders that were conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Dragan Obrenovic spent that night, the night between the 12th and the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic was at the command. He came that evening. During the day, he came and went. And that night, he spent at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you hand over your duties as duty operations officer on the 13th and to whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th, I handed over my duty to the assistant for logistics, Sreten Milosevic, at around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The handing over, was it conducted in accordance with the rules that you described to us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I informed him about everything, the procedure that was implemented was the one regulated by the rules. He took over. I was supposed to have a day off that day. And after I handed over my duties, I did not go home, but rather stayed at the command in accordance with the orders of the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any significant activities of movements of units that morning, on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning, on the 13th of July, a unit assembled. I think it was an ad hoc unit. There were about 25 soldiers from another battalion, about 15 members of the engineering company. Then we also had some donors there, 12 to 15. Then we had a logistics platoon from our brigade, about 15 to 20 people altogether. And I think that the chief of staff ordered them to go to Snagovo sector in order to protect Serbian villages in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of that ad hoc unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most senior officer, the only one who was there, and that was Dragan Jevtic. He was the commander of the engineering company who had a group of -- who was leading a group of about 15 members of the engineering unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you spend the morning or the afternoon hours of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the command on the 13th. I went to sleep, to have some rest. And in the afternoon, I think it was 5.00 or 6.00 p.m., I received a call from the chief of staff. He asked me to come to his office and ordered me to go in a vehicle to Snagovo to find the unit that had been sent up there because allegedly Jevtic couldn't really carry out his duties, was unable to organise that. It was obvious that that wasn't a combat unit, that had not seen combat before and that he was experiencing some problems with the unit. And at around 6.00 p.m., I drove in a vehicle to Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what vehicle you drove in?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was an Opel Record. Acimovic was the driver. I know that -- I remember that he was also scared. He didn't really want to drive because the road had been blocked for the past 24 hours. However, we did set out anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you went from the command of the Zvornik Brigade to Snagovo, did you have to pass through Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. From Rasica in Karakaj, one would take the asphalt road through Orahovac bypassing the settlement itself, taking the highway. And then you would go to Crni Vrh, and then from Crni Vrh, you would turn left on the macadam road and continue on to Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what time it was on the 13th when you passed through Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was before the dark. I think that it was around 6.00 or 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That was a misstatement of the evidence. He did not pass through Snagovo, he passed through on the main road, bypassing -- sorry, Orahovac. He didn't pass through Orahovac; he bypassed it on the main road. Given what was going on in Orahovac at the time, that's a very important distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that you have been to that location. For us, I have never been there. I don't know how that roadway, whether it runs past, through the city, or just bypass it. Mr. Stojanovic, would you please be more specific on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I sincerely hope that you will be able to see it for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you say "I passed through Orahovac," did you mean that you passed through the village of Orahovac? This asphalt road that you were taking, did it actually go through the settlement itself, through Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main road has a sign saying "Orahovac," meaning the settlement of Orahovac. And the main road does pass through the settlement; however, before an overpass, there is a turn where -- which you can take if you want to go into the settlement itself, which would be some 500 metres away from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that road, is there a tavern called Nedjina Kafana?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. Before the railway overpass, where there's a turn to take to the village, on the right some 30 to 40 metres away, there are two shops. One of them is actually a tavern, the so-called Nedjina Kafana.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Driving at a normal speed, how long would you need to travel from Snagovo to the command of the Zvornik Brigade? How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking this road that I described, one wouldn't need more than 25 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What about the intersection where you turn to Snagovo, the intersection where you take the macadam road leading to Crni Vrh, how long would you need to get to there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now ask the usher to assist us so that we can show the witness a map showing the area the witness has just spoken about. And we will show the Court the notes that Witness Milan Maric entered into the map of that we were able to see yesterday which was used during the interview he gave to the investigators of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you can, Mr. Maric, could you please use the pointer to indicate on the map which is on the ELMO, very briefly, the direction or the route from Zvornik, from the brigade command to Snagovo where you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we seem to be having a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg for a little patience. Thank you. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, if you could please indicate with a pointer on the map which is on the ELMO what route you took that evening from the Zvornik Brigade command to the crossroads for Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Zvornik Brigade we took the asphalt road as far as Karakaj. Then we took the main road as far as Crni Vrh. From there, we took the dirt road or macadam road to Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show us where Orahovac is located or the Lazete location as marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the place. To the right is the road leading to the village of Orahovac itself. This is the railway overpass, and the tavern is some 40 metres from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this area, in the evening of the 13th, did you see any unusual activity, any movement of vehicles or anything similar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was driving along this road, there were no activities, no soldiers. In Orahovac, the road was blocked, it was closed off. Here there were civilian police, and the road was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say there was an obstacle placed there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a wooden obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And were you stopped at that obstacle?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. They told me that the road was blocked, that I couldn't take that road. But I told them that I had orders from the commander to pass along that road, and then they removed the obstacle, and I was able to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please show us where you went, where you met up with Dragan Jevtic and the units that were there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met up with Dragan Jevtic in the area of Snagovo on the road. This is where I found them all gathered together in that place. I saw what the problems were. And then I deployed the soldiers in such a way that they could defend themselves most effectively. The inhabitants of the village were also there. They were upset. They were afraid. And that evening, I received information that a unit of the special purpose police from Doboj was to come and join up with us. It was to be brought there by Ljubo Bojanovic. So we waited for that unit to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to say that the map we are using for purposes of identification is marked D132/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that evening or during that night between the 13th and the 14th, were there any intense combat activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't engage in any combat, the unit that was in the Snagovo area. But we could hear sporadic fire coming from the 7th and 4th Battalions. But I don't think there was any intensive fighting anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To your left-hand side in the direction of the village of Maricici and Zvornik, were there any units belonging to you, your army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the east in the direction of Zvornik, there were no units of ours. And that's where we were expecting Ljubo Bojanovic who was to bring a special purpose police unit from Doboj. As far as I know, at Kula Grad near Zvornik, there were civilian policemen securing that area. But I didn't see that. It was quite far off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please use the pointer to indicate on the map to your right this empty area where Maricici, Kula Grad, and Zvornik are located.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an empty area stretching as far as Zvornik. This is the Maricici area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And Kula Grad?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So at Kula Grad there were civilian policemen, and from there to your left flank, there was no one?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, there was no one there. And we had 50 to 60 men which means that -- well, in military terms, they were poorly equipped with no combat experience, without any support, without any proper positions in the woods so that the situation was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That morning or that night, between the 13th and the 14th, did the police from Doboj arrive and did you link up with them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubo Bojanovic did bring a group. I think it was between 200 and 250 special-purpose policemen from Doboj. And he joined up with us just before dawn. I think it might have been 4.00 a.m. And then we linked up, and this was the area that they -- where they took up positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That morning or that night, just before dawn, did you personally meet Ljubo Bojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. For them to come along that road from Maricici to avoid any surprises, I took a group of soldiers and went a kilometre, kilometre and a half ahead to meet them. So I met them personally, and then we brought them back and linked them up with our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To whom was this police unit subordinated in military terms? Were they acting on their own or in coordination or on the command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This unit arrived at the request probably of our brigade. It was sent by the Main Staff. And as soon as they arrived in our territory, they were automatically resubordinated to the most responsible commander in this area. That was their task which they received from the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And who at that point was in command of all these units, both your unit and the police unit? Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the chief, Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This may be a good time to ask you. On that day, the 13th, while you were in the command of the Zvornik Brigade, did you see Dragan Jokic there at all and was he active in any way? Did he have any tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Dragan Jokic at all on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me until when you had contact with and physically saw Dragan Obrenovic at Snagovo on the 13th and during the night between the 13th and the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Dragan Obrenovic when he issued the order to me that I should go to Snagovo. And the next time I saw him was on the 14th. I think it was around 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: In the night between the 13th and the 14th, did you see him at Snagovo at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He wasn't at Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you tell us whether you know until when you were with Ljubo Bojanovic and how long he stayed in Maricici and Snagovo, in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubo Bojanovic brought the troops, linked up with us. And immediately after that, he got lost. I didn't see him again. He wasn't in that area. Whether he went back or where he went, I don't know. I didn't see him after that in the Snagovo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the morning of the 14th, were there any events, any contacts with the armed column of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning of the 14th, the soldiers took prisoner two Muslim scouts who were on their way back from the Federation area, not from Srebrenica, but from the Nezuk area in the opposite direction. These were young men aged between 18 and 25. And they were wearing civilian clothes and not carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, you said they were coming from the area of the 2nd Corps of the BH Army going in the direction of the column that was leaving Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were caught when they were returning from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who took these two men prisoner, these two Muslims? Which soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which soldiers they were, whether they were from the group I mentioned or from the special-purpose police unit. When I was touring the men I had deployed at certain positions, I saw those two prisoners. And that was when the chief of staff arrived, around 8.00 or 9.00. I was present when these prisoners were questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And who questioned these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of staff personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And who was the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of staff was Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you present during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was there while the prisoners were being questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember what they were asked about and what they said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief wanted to know where they had come from, whose couriers they were, how many Muslims there were, what direction they were moving in, how many of them had weapons, how far away they were from us, in what areas they were. This was all intelligence information. And let me mention that on that morning, an officer was there, Milos Petkovic, from the intelligence organ, and there was a group of military policemen with him. There was a major there as well. I think his name was Zoran who had brought a special unit from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this might be a good time for a break. I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, yesterday you promised us you only needed 20 minutes to finish the direct examination. Now, we have been here for over an hour. So I believe that your direct examination could be streamlined. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, we will cover the events more quickly now, and let us focus on the 14th and 15th, which is relevant for our Defence. Please allow me to remind you that before the break, we got to the morning of the 14th and the conversation with the three prisoners of war. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened after that and what you remember as characteristic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, while the prisoners of war were being questioned, Zoran Jovanovic came, the operations officer from the brigade, and he brought a group of 50 to 60 soldiers as reinforcement. Then, in that period, I noticed two prisoners who had surrendered to the military police. They were boarded on to a truck. I also saw a couple of soldiers boarding the truck. I think that these were two soldiers from the engineers, from Dragan Jevtic's unit, about three or four donors. And I could see a small number of people leaving. I asked Jevtic, "Where are you going? Where are these people going?" And he said: "Under Obrenovic's orders, we're leaving." Obrenovic was there. He was about 10 metres away from where this was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you know that these were two engineers who were leaving? Did you know them personally or did somebody tell you that two engineers were leaving the lines?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that Jevtic was angry. And I asked him, he waved his hand. And he said that it was under Obrenovic's orders that two of his engineers were leaving. He didn't tell me where they were going or why, and I don't know whether he knew that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because of the intercepts that I'm going to show you later. In these activities when the engineers were released, did you have any tasks or duties or did you take part in this in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't know about the order, nor who approved this. But I saw that Obrenovic was there. I didn't question anything. He was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This example, does that illustrate what we talked about in the rules? Did Dragan Jevtic as commander of the engineering company have to act in accordance with orders of the chief of staff and release these two engineers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, if he received an order from the chief of staff to do so; he could have released the whole unit, the chief of staff. So Jevtic would have to agree to carry out this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Dragan Jokic anywhere there? Or did you have any communication with him on that day, on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Dragan Jokic that day either. And I didn't have any communication with him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That day, Dragan Jokic was the duty operations officer at the Zvornik Brigade. Did you have the opportunity to have any kind of radio communications with the duty operations officer, Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any need, and I didn't call the duty operations officer for anything. We didn't talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened then on the 14th in the evening, in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we finished with the prisoners, the chief ordered the unit to organise itself and to start to search the terrain ahead in order to go towards the column that was coming in. Up until about 1800 hours, the deployment proceeded. Zoran's men, the military police, they were being deployed. And they began to search the terrain. Around 1800 or 1830 hours, we clashed with the column of Muslims. It was quite an intense clash. The fighting didn't last very long, perhaps for about half an hour or so or an hour. Then there was sporadic fire afterwards. Many of our fighters were killed at that time. There were ones who were captured as well, and you could hear on the radio that the commander, Major Zoran, from the command was captured. He was the one who had brought the civilian police, the special police from Doboj. And they were asking for a halt of the fire. The fire was halted later. We continued to pull out our forces which had dispersed in contact with the enemy, and this pullout went on until quite late into the night, until about 2300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were these intense combat operations? Were there intense exchanges? Was the fighting intense?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The clash itself was quite intense with a lot of casualties, with a lot of killed and wounded, and many of our soldiers were captured alive. This was then followed by sporadic fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This combat column of the 28th Division, did it manage to break through and continue along on its way? What happened with them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening, this column passed by. It passed through our defence that we had set up. And then it crossed the asphalt road. The Caparde-Zvornik main road. They passed through the sector of Planinci, Perunike-Planinci, and continued on towards Krizevici, towards the 4th Battalion, towards Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, how far was the Zvornik Brigade first line of defence away, far away from the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The front section of our defence was about 4 kilometres away from the incoming column.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night between the 14th and the 15th of July after this fighting which took place on the 14th in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evening between the 14th and the 15th, I spent in the village of Snagovo. It was about -- near the Stara Skola sector. We didn't know what had happened to about 40 of our soldiers. It started to rain. There was a storm. And we spent the night holding those positions around the Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you if you remember whether you saw Dragan Obrenovic at any point that night when you were at Snagovo; and if you did, where and when did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we pulled out from the battle, I saw Dragan Obrenovic. He was on the asphalt road in the village of Snagovo, and I saw him that night. He was waiting to see exactly what had happened to the soldiers, to see what the outcome of the combat operations was. He was at Snagovo with us until midnight. He had his own vehicle, but he was also walking along the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you see him after that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I saw Obrenovic in the morning at dawn. He was also in a vehicle. And then we continued to follow the tracks of the Muslim column that had passed by. We reached Perunike, and that is where the armoured personnel carrier went to the Crni Vrh sector with Major Krunic and the most capable men. Some of the personnel, together with me, went to Planinci, down to the asphalt road, and that is where we encountered one of our fighters from the 7th Battalion, Dusko, who had gone to Zvornik that night with the medical corps. He was very happy to see us. He kissed us. He said that we had saved him. He said that the medical personnel had gone to Zvornik. There were many wounded that night, and they ran into a Muslim ambush set up by the Muslims who were passing along that road. The driver and the male nurse were killed. He managed to save himself. We sent him up to Perunike because Obrenovic stayed up there. And we reported back to our people in the brigade to send some medical staff and ambulances to gather the corpses. Afterwards, at around 9.00 or 10.00, when I went back to Perunike, Obrenovic was no longer there, and I didn't see him since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let us then summarise this. From the 14th at night to early in the morning on the 15th, you did not see Obrenovic. You saw him again in the morning on the 15th. And then until 10.00 of the 15th when you came back to Perunike, he had already left. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reached Perunike --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading. On this topic, leading should not be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, I think that's the difference between the two legal systems about the direct examinations. And in these proceedings, there's no need for the counsel to sum up whatever the witness said. The Judges will read the transcript and arrive at his own conclusions. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I didn't have any intention to do so. I just wanted to complete this topic. But let us continue. I think that this will not be in dispute anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened then on the 15th in the afternoon, Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th, in the afternoon, the self-propelled gun remained with Commander Tacka. The Muslim stragglers, the forces were passing by us. There was sporadic fire that was being exchanged at a certain point. Two or three uniformed members of the column were captured. We later found their weapons. And sometime in the afternoon, I think it was perhaps around 1700 hours, the commander, Pandurevic, asked me where I was and ordered me to stay there at that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this your first contact via radio with Pandurevic on that day, on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first contact, so that's when I spoke with Pandurevic, on the 15th at around 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was already in the Zvornik Brigade area of defence at that time? Could you conclude where he was, at which position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on our conversation, I concluded that he was in the Zvornik sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you explain to him the difficulties of your position, the fact that you were there with just a small number of soldiers there in the Perunike region?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I tried to explain to him to tell him that I was left with very few soldiers there and that I wanted to leave that area and join up with the nearest unit. And he ordered me explicitly to remain in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on that, did you conclude that he had taken over command over the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He took over command over the brigade. He took over that post from Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that from that moment on, you were to follow his orders to remain in the position in which you were at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point just now, you said that that afternoon on the 15th, there were also two or three soldiers from the column who had been captured. What happened to them? Who processed them, so to speak? Who interrogated them? What treatment were they given?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers received fair treatment. They were fed. I don't think that there was any interrogation going on because we were in a situation where we had no time for that, nor would we have somebody to pass this information on. We couldn't hand them over to anyone else because there was no police there, there were no other units of ours there. It was raining that night. And the prisoners spent that night with us. We organised some kind of a circular defence around the self-propelled vehicle, and the prisoners were there with us. In the morning, the soldiers were fine.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the prisoners were fine.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I asked the commander to join up with Zoran and his people, and I was told to go down to Kamenolom, to the quarry which is right below Perunike. In the morning hours, that's exactly what we did. We descended down there. Zoran's people were not there. We were told that they were way down below, and we continued on until we came upon our soldiers. I found Zoran at the terrace of Nedjina Kafana, the tavern, and I handed over the prisoners there. There were people from our military police there, and I think that they had already had three other prisoners. These prisoners were not mistreated, although yes, they were bound. We handed over our prisoners to the military police. Then the troops from the logistics company of our brigade were returned from the barracks because they had escaped. Pandurevic returned them. So I went to drive them to their positions to the hill on the left from the road leading to quarry. I stayed there for some two hours. And upon my return - I was really tired at that point - I went back to Zoran. I saw that there were no troops there, no military police, no prisoners. I asked Zoran what happened to them. And Zoran replied that he was told that they had gone to Zvornik with military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Everything that you just told us, does this pertain to the 16th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 16th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this for the following reason: We have already heard many witnesses here, and it has become a fact that in the evening hours on the 14th of July in Orahovac, mass executions of prisoners were carried out. In the night between the 14th and the 15th, prisoners were executed in Petkovci village, in Crveni Mulj, dam. So in those days on the 15th and 16th, did you know that in your rear as the combat was going on, the executions were also being carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, and I think the same applies to all other people who were with me because they were fighting for their lives on their positions. The combat was quite intense at the front section in the area of defence of those battalions. Therefore, we couldn't even have assumed what was going on elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that calls for conclusion, especially as to the Dragan Jevtic who has released engineers earlier. He can't possibly know what's in his mind unless he has some more evidence than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think the witness has already answered that question, and we'll take into consideration your objections when we elaborate on that piece of the evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, how far was it from the positions where you were on the 14th, 15th, and 16th to the Crveni Mulj dam in Petkovci or in the sector of the Petkovci village?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crveni Mulj dam is some 7 kilometres from that area as the crow flies, 6 to 7 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And how far is it from the positions where you were at Crni Vrh or in Snagovo to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you return to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to the brigade on the 17th. Commander Pandurevic gave me a day off. I went home. On the 18th, I returned back to the brigade and received an order to go with a group of military police, special police from Doboj, to the sector of the 4th Battalion, Kitovnice, to search the terrain there as they could still hear sporadic fire aimed at our positions behind our backs. So we were busy with this search during which time two of our soldiers were killed as a result of an ambush. We discontinued further searching without defeating those forces which then withdrew back to their depth. And I returned back to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During this search, did you capture any soldiers of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any prisoners. Their forces withdrew to their depth, back to the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember whether that was on the 18th or the 19th of July, if you had a day off before that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 18th. I think I went to the brigade on the 17th and had that day off, and that this happened on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Vinko Pandurevic already the commander of the brigade at that time, did he have full command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vinko Pandurevic was in full command. He was physically present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now turn to the period after the war. After the war, did you remain with the Zvornik Brigade as an active serviceman?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After these events, I remained with the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And for how long did you remain with the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained with the Zvornik Brigade until the establishment of the Manoeuvre Brigade. I went to the Manoeuvre Brigade from the Drina Corps, and I was demobilised from that brigade on the 20th of April 1996. For a time I worked in a company. At the request of senior officers, the commander, I returned to Zvornik Brigade as a professional soldier and continued working there until 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What rank did you hold then, Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rank of major. The rank of captain first class was discontinued, and I received the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go on to work from there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked at the staff. I was officer for teaching and training. I also worked as intelligence officer. After the departure of Dusko Vukotic, I was appointed to that post. And as Obrenovic was preparing his defence, as I've said yesterday, when he asked for an alibi for me for the 13th and 14th, I couldn't confirm that he was with me. Following these events, I was transferred to the corps command, although my family lives in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us pause here for a moment. I didn't quite understand when you said that Obrenovic asked for an alibi from you. What did he actually ask from you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As he was preparing his defence - everybody knew that he was preparing his defence for quite some time - he was calling senior officers who at the time were holding such posts so that they could help him. That included Ljubo Bojanovic, myself, Ostoja Stanisic, Lazar Ristic, Milan Stanojevic, Momir Jasikovac. I know what discussions he had with me. He asked for an alibi to cover the 12th, the 13th, and the 14th to ascertain where he was and what he did. During the conversation, he stated that issued orders for me to go to Perunike via telephone and that he hadn't given those orders to me in the office. I said that wasn't true, that he gave those orders to me in the office. Then he said he was present with me the whole time when Ljubo Bojanovic brought in people. I also said that wasn't true because I only saw him in the morning when he was questioning witnesses. And then he said, "Well, where else could I have been?" And I said, "I don't know about that." He was uncomfortable, and one could notice that. And he said to me that I should refresh my memory and that he would come back and talk to me later about this. In the meantime, I was transferred to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These words that Obrenovic uttered to you asking you to refresh your memory and that he would come back and talk to you again, did you see that as a warning that you should provide an alibi for him for the 13th and the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take it as a threat; I simply saw that he was searching through the papers, preparing his defence, trying to recollect the events. And I thought that through that he was trying to achieve something. And then I asked Ljubo Bojanovic because I want to verify my own recollections, whether he had seen him in the forest as he was passing through, and Ljubo said no, he didn't see him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were presenting your defence to the investigators of the Tribunal, did you inform them about these facts relating to the conduct of Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the topics of our conversation. And yes, I informed them about these facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also say to them then that you thought that there was the reason for your transfer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that to them because I saw no reason for me to be transferred from Zvornik to Sokolac. That was a sort of a punishment for me and for my family, a degradation, a full degradation in the sense of the work that I'd been doing until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Something remained unclear, so let me try to clarify that. What post did Dragan Obrenovic have in that period of time, 1999 to 2000?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, Obrenovic was commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The people that you've mentioned, the officers, Ostoja Stanisic, Lazar Ristic, Milan Stanojevic, commander of military police company Momir Jasikovac, were they still members of that unit whose commander he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of these people that you mentioned are not with the army any more. They have gone on to other jobs. They are not professional servicemen any more. And based on his request, they came to see him at his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see them coming into his office? Where were you sitting at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I dealt with operations duties. And it's on the same floor, the last office on that floor. And there's a hallway leading to commander and the chief of staff. When these conversations were conducted, people from military police were always present. And nobody else could enter the office at the time except for those who were invited to go and see the commander. The door normally used to be always open, so I was able to see everyone coming in while I was in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were transferred to Sokolac, did you find Dragan Jokic there? Was he also transferred there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Jokic went there six months or a year before I did, and we were transferred to the same organ. I arrived in the same organ where Dragan Jokic was already working.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Dragan Jokic's family living in Zvornik at the time, like yours?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Jokic's family also lived in Zvornik, just like my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who Dragan lived with and who his family members were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jokic had a son and a mother in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he had a wife? Was he married? Who took care of the child?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not living with his wife. He didn't have a wife. And I think he was the one who took care both of the child and of his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you say that in spite of this family situation, he, too, was transferred to Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was transferred to Sokolac, and he went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you work together with Dragan at Sokolac in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We worked together in the same organ, the operative training department of the 5th Corps until he went to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you practically have to share living quarters as you were far from your hometown?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a while we were roommates in the hotel at Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
