utterances.text: Mr. Maric, when you were alone with Dragan, did you have an opportunity to discuss all the tragic events that had taken place in Zvornik, to comment on them, to wonder what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions, I asked Jokic whether he knew about those events, especially after the information that came to light during the Krstic trial which we learned through the media. I asked him whether he knew anything about this, whether he had taken part in it and so on. I never got a reply to the effect that he had participated or known about anything that was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If this is speculation, you may object. But how did you come to this conclusion, or rather, what was your conclusion about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Vague. What conclusion and what does "this" mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think the witness answered, "I never got a reply to the effect that he had participated or known about anything that was going on at that time." To me, it's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I withdraw this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me conclude with the following question: Mr. Maric, do you know that in the period 2000-2001, an investigation was carried out in Vlasenica about individual criminal acts in the Zvornik Brigade against certain members of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I don't know about any investigations in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would just like briefly to go through the documents referring to your testimony. And I will only ask you for brief comments on these. Could you please assist me in this way. I would like to show you excerpts from the duty officers' logbook, the logbook. That's P133. And it refers to the period from the 12th of July when this witness was the duty operations officer. We have already had several opportunities to see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, just for clarification, I believe witnesses and other people have been referring to this as the duty officer notebook, if this is the handwritten jottings that you're referring to, because there's another logbook as well. So if we could just try to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. This is the notebook kept by the duty operations officer in the command of the Zvornik Brigade. And this is P533.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: P533, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, I apologise for this brief delay. But let us try to clarify this. Is this the book of notes kept by the duty operations officer on the 12th of July, and were you the duty operations officer on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, do you recognise your handwriting in this notebook and from which note does your handwriting actually begin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My handwriting begins from 09 -- what's this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you at least read us this note?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Milosevic should go up there or send what he promised, and he should be there by 12.30." And then "584-700." This is a telephone number. The telephone number of Glinica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Above this note, it says "Trbic to the forward command post." Can you assist us in explaining what actually these notes refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting. This was noted down by somebody who was in the shift before mine. And it means that Trbic was at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the forward command post had already been established?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As duty officers, we were not told it would be taken. But apparently, the commander decided it should be taken, and he probably sent Trbic to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We have a note here, "Situation normal, Palma 2," on the first page. Mr. Maric, it's in Cyrillic. "Situation normal, Palma 2." Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is this? Is it yours?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period from 9.20, "Petkovic should go to fetch the Muslims in the 8th Infantry Battalion." This is already my handwriting, and this other handwriting belongs to Ljubo Bojanovic. I was probably absent either because I had been given an assignment or I was touring the premises. And this is his handwriting. He wrote this down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us who Palma 2 is. What could this refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think our brigade was Palma, but I'm not sure whether it was Palma 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's pass on to page 2, ERN number in B/C/S 02935733. Is this your handwriting, Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 733, that page? Yes, yes, it's all in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It says, "Petkovic to go and fetch the Muslims in the 8th Infantry Battalion." Is this the information you mentioned during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The chief of staff ordered that Petkovic should go and fetch the Muslims from the 8th Infantry Battalion, and this message was transmitted to Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After this, there is the text of a telegram. Can you tell us what this is about, what sort of telegram is this? What is the content of this letter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the telegram I mentioned during my testimony when I said that the chief had dictated a telegram to me to be sent off to all the units, to all the units except the 6th Infantry Battalion. Should I read it all out?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, you don't have to do that. I just wanted to ask you briefly through this example, where at this time was the chief of staff when you were writing out this text?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was standing right next to me and dictating what I wrote down. He then signed the telegram, and it was sent off to the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this an example of what you were talking about this morning, about the method of dispatching regular and interim combat reports? Was this the method used as a rule?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, yes. The chief dictated this, and that's how it was sent to all the addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You're trying to say that he was present and he was dictating; you were just writing down?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection,.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Leading and multiple part. It's impossible to tell what the witness means by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: After all, Mr. Stojanovic, I believe the witness has already answered that question. There's no need to repeat it once again. You may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, on the following page, B/C/S ERN number 02935735, there is another note that says "Palma 2, at 1330," and then there is a text. Was this text written by you? Is it your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you look at the content of this note, can you tell us who Palma 2 might be?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's our communications centre, but it probably arrived through our communications centre. People are asking Vukotic what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And as far as I'm concerned, we're finished with this document. Now, I would like to show you some pages from the same document on days when you were not the duty officer, but your name was mentioned. Let us try to decipher those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for identification, this is still Prosecution Exhibit P133, the duty operation officers notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May I ask you first to look at the excerpt from this notebook, ERN number in English 03089341, and in the B/C/S, it's 02935746. Mr. Maric, this is part of the notes noted down by Dragan Jokic who was the duty officer at the time. And on the page, it says "PC, 1st C, Maric, and then there's a list, 30-2nd pb, 35-2nd pb, and then there's donors, 15 engineers, and so on. Can you tell us what this is about? What kind of entry is this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an entry showing probably what units were supposed to be at the positions at Snagovo. This is what was supposed to happen, but that's not what happened in reality. Whoever dictated this thought that there should be that number of men there, 30 from the 2nd Infantry Battalion, 35 from the 2nd Infantry Battalion, 15 from the engineers, and so on and so forth, but in actual fact the situation on the ground did not correspond to these numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this record is simply not correct about the number of people who went to Snagovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. This is not correct. This information is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the duty operations officer only wrote down into the notebook something that someone else dictated to him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He writes down into the notebook what he receives over the telephone. Over the telephone or if he was told it in person or via the communications centre. Messages, orders, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to move to the next page. In the English version, that is 03089354; and in the B/C/S version, it's 02935759. Mr. Maric, this is a duty operations officer's note from the 16th of July 1995. I want to ask you, do you know who was the duty operations officer on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The last entry on this page states: "Bring spare batteries to Maric at Crni Vrh for the RU and the RUP12." Could you please explain to us what this is, what does this entry mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this unit was up there from the 13th, already on the 14th in the afternoon, the battery on the radio device was weakened. And the communications were being established via the 7th Infantry Battalion with the brigade command, or from the self-propelled vehicle. The last conversation that I had with Pandurevic on the 15th in the evening came practically at the end of the life of the battery, so we had remained without communication. So that was the meaning of this entry, to take the spare batteries to Maric at Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you allow me to look at another excerpt from the same notebook, from the same exhibit, P133. And in the English version, it's the ERN 30889371; and in the B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the number of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I just wanted to repeat the ERN number. That is 02935776.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an entry of the duty operations officer for the 18th of July. Mr. Maric, do you know maybe who was the duty operations officer on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was out in the field. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It states here: "Maric and Zoran to have one day off each." Could you please tell us what this entry is about. Who is Zoran and who is being given the day off?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran and I when we returned to the brigade together that morning, Commander Pandurevic gave us a day off each. And we went home. That's what that means, "Maric and Zoran to have one day off."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Zoran," which Zoran do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations officer in the same section where I was working, Zoran Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this entry mean that the commander gave you your days off and not the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. The commander was the one who would give or approve days off. The duty operations officer could not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the job of the duty operations officer is just to record what the commander said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am going to show you one more document that we have already used here before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask the usher to show it to you. This is the collection of the Dekici intercepted conversations, and this is Exhibit P121.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, could you please look at page 3 of the B/C/S version. And for ID purposes, this is ERN number 00848952 in B/C/S. And the English version has been provided earlier to the Court and to the Prosecution. We already used it yesterday. So it's the same copy. Mr. Maric, could you please briefly comment on this. There is a conversation between Lovac 1 and Lovac. And it says the following: "Are you in communication with Maric?" Answer: "Yes. Zolka has left. Someone should be sent there to meet the people." And then there is a note for Maric, Miladinovic, and Mitrovic "(engineers should go to Nedjina Kafana with a dredger so they could cut through the road)." Could you briefly explain to us who is Lovac, who is Lovac 1, and who is communicating to whom here, and is your name mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lovac 1 is the chief of staff, and he's addressing Lovac, that is the switchboard, the communications centre whether they were in communication with me, and he said that they were, that Zoran had left, Zoran Jovanovic had gone up there with his men and to send somebody up there to get those people for Maric, Miladinovic, Mitrovic, and the engineers are supposed to go to the dredger to cut through the road. The contents of this telegram are familiar. Maric never arrived. This is the chief of staff sending a telegram to Maric, to me, that these two engineers should come to the Nedjina Kafana with an excavator to cut through the road. Perhaps this reached the unit, but according to what you could see when those two engineers left, as I mentioned, when they boarded that truck as I said before, Obrenovic himself was there, and when I asked Jevtic, "Where are these people going?" He said, "They are going under orders of Obrenovic." So probably this is that telegram that two engineers should be released to go and do something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on a conversation like this, can you tell us perhaps where Lovac 1 was at that time when he was asking Lovac, "Are you in communication with Maric?" "I have." And then repeats: "Zolka has left." Who is Zolka, and where did he go to and where did he leave from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zolka is Zoran Jovanovic, a major in the operations sector who was supposed to take the people up there to help out the unit that I was with. And he was probably calling from the barracks because he received information, and he was asked if he was in communication with me. And he said that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us just stay here for a second. You're saying he's informing. Are you thinking of Lovac 1? Are you thinking of Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, he was in the barracks, and he was informing about Zolka's departure. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. First of all, there was complete speculation on where Obrenovic was. He says "probably," and then again we have the same questioning of the Defence attorney saying, confirming that is a leading question and putting it to the witness. That's terribly leading on what was a speculative, conclusory answer. That's inappropriate and improper because it leaves the record in a shambles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. And I think there's still some room for improvement in this set of questions, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to finish with this question, Your Honour, and I think that I will finish my examination-in-chief also with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Maric, did you in any way participate in the decision why Mitrovic and Miladinovic, the engineers were supposed to go to Nedjina Kafana with an excavator?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any information about them. I didn't know if they were the operators of this machinery. I didn't know where they were supposed to go. I didn't receive this telegram. I simply saw that the people were leaving the positions and that two few people remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Maric. Your Honour, I have no further questions. Mr. Maric, I will ask you to concentrate a little bit longer and to respond to questions from Mr. Karnavas and from Mr. McCloskey. On behalf of our Defence team, I thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Karnavas, do you have questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But I won't be overtaxing the witness. In other words, there are a few, but we won't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we have a break first. Then we'll come back to your...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I just have a few questions, and I want to -- about four different topics. First of all -- and I'll go in the order in which they were presented on direct. You indicated to us that you had studied political science, and in more particular, you had specialised in All People's Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I completed the political science faculty, the department for All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just briefly, because this concept has come up, and it's one of the key issues, I think that we're trying to resolve. But could you tell us a little bit about what is All People's Defence? What is this concept about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What scope? What scope?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think, you know, Mr. Karnavas is doing the direct examination at this moment. And we'll allow Mr. Karnavas to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept of All People's Defence was a doctrinal principle of organising and planning and carrying out combat operations within an all people's defence or defensive war. Under the doctrinal principle on the use of units, the organisation of the sociopolitical system under the circumstances where the armed forces were organised in such a way following the instructions. At the end of this training course, after completing the faculty for All People's Defence, one would receive a title of a professor in the area of All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, with that title as professor, where would you teach this concept of All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our education system, a professor for All People's Defence would teach in all secondary schools. He would teach the subject called All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in some countries such as the one I come from, students get to choose courses. Was this an optional course? In other words, could students decide not to take this particular course, the course of All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In our system, this was a mandatory course taught in all secondary schools. It was taught throughout all four years of secondary schooling, whereas in vocational schools it was taught in the last two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was that course offered to boys as well as girls?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was taught to both boys and girls. It was a mandatory course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you tell us why it was important to teach this course for four years to high-school, secondary-school students?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept that existed before the war was the concept aimed at preparing the population for a defensive war, not an offensive war. Therefore, in that framework, the youth was also prepared for that, including the girls who were not expected to serve military service, whereas the boys were to be prepared in order to serve their service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The concept of territorial defence, was that part of the All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Territorial defence was part of armed forces. Therefore, in addition to the Yugoslav People's Army as a military force, we also had territorial defence as part of armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about civil protection, civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian protection was not part of armed forces. It was a part of civilian structure, and it had different tasks; namely, to protect the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was that also encompassed within this principle or this doctrine of All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Civilian protection was also one of the courses at the faculty for All People's Defence. So it was taught within that course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And lastly, regarding this topic, you were asked some questions about mobilisation of buses. Was that part of this concept of All People's Defence, the ability of the military or the government, the ministries, to be able to mobilise sectors of the civilian population to assist in times of emergencies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The ministry or the government were able to mobilise resources from other structures which were not within the armed forces but were needed for the armed forces. Therefore, in extraordinary circumstances, in wartime, certain resources could be mobilised and allocated to those who needed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me go on to the next topic. You indicated, and correct me if I'm wrong, that on the night of the 13th going on to the 14th, that Mr. Bojanovic, Ljubo Bojanovic, had brought some special police, I believe, from Doboj. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He brought in a unit of special police which was -- which existed within the MUP. They came from Doboj via the request that was sent through the General Staff. They came to our area pursuant to our request to assist us in combat operations. They were brought in by Ljubo Bojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what his function was within the Zvornik Brigade, Ljubo Bojanovic's?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, Ljubo Bojanovic was operations officer in an operations organ, just like I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now we have a statement from a Prosecution witness, Witness 130, I won't reveal his name, who has indicated that on the 13th, Mr. Bojanovic was also serving as the duty operations officer. To your knowledge, was Ljubo Bojanovic the duty operation officer on the 13th of July, that same day that he came into the field where you were located and brought the special police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, I handed over my duty to Sreten Milosevic, assistant for logistics. And he was supposed to be the duty operations officer. He took over from me. I don't think that Ljubo Bojanovic was the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe you can clarify this point: When one is designated as the duty operations officer, is he allowed to leave that position and go out in the field, be elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is allowed, but under certain circumstances when ordered either by the commander or the chief of staff. Then he can leave his duty post, but another person, another officer, is designated as a replacement while he's gone. The replacement officer comes from the list of duty officers and is picked among those who are located in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Suffice it to say at all times there is somebody there at the operations office acting as the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At all times, a duty officer is present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to switch to another topic, and that was with respect to Mr. Obrenovic. I just want to nail down one specific point. You had indicated that at some point, Mr. Obrenovic had come up to you asking for an alibi, or what would appear to be an alibi as you understood it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When he asked me to come into his office to talk to him, that was taking place in his office. Based on our conversation, I concluded that he wanted an alibi at a certain time, at a certain place. He wanted it to be known where he was and what he did. That was the sense of our conversation. He said that he issued an order to me on the telephone, that he was not present in the barracks, and that in the night between the 13th and 14th, he was with me on the positions and that he was with me when Ljubo brought in the special police unit. Based on that, I concluded that. And I knew from before that he was working on preparing his defence because he had already received a summons from The Hague investigators, and he was preparing for new calls from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And from the line of questioning and the manner in which he spoke to you and the information that he provided to you, it's my understanding, and correct me if I'm wrong, that he was attempting to influence your memory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. In our conversation, I saw that he was uncomfortable. And he said, "Well, where could I have been? Where else could I have been? I was there. Try and rattle your memory."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then at some point after this incident, you were questioned by the Prosecution, and as I believe you indicated that was one of the focal points of the Prosecution; that is, Obrenovic trying to influence you as far as the recitation of events of where he had been on what given days and in what places?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on conversations with other colleagues who were in the army then and with whom Obrenovic talked, one could conclude that Obrenovic talked to them about the same topic. He wanted them to say what he had told them in any conversations they had with investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I suspect by now, you do know that the Prosecution came into court using your statement as a basis of trying to demonstrate that Mr. Obrenovic was out trying to influence witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, it's a very difficult question for this witness to speculate the strategy of the Prosecution. It's not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, it's not the strategy of the Prosecution, but I'm merely trying to establish that the Prosecution had a great deal of confidence in the gentleman's testimony with respect to that issue, and therefore later on they shouldn't be in a position to argue that his testimony should be less credible on other aspects. Because that was the basis for Mr. Obrenovic not being able to get provisionally released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, for this kind of thing to be said in front of the witness, we all remember those days. We know where the Prosecution stood. And this is all argument. And I have no objection to the questioning on this point. As it appears, the witness is telling Mr. Karnavas exactly what he told us. But the rest of the strategy and these other absurd arguments are not relevant and inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that later on, on closing argument, I don't want to hear any statements that this particular witness is less than credible on other issues such as All People's Defence just to give an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this kind of argument at this point, we will be arguing that this witness is less than credible on other events as we will hear from the cross-examination. I just hope that if these kind of arguments are going to be made, they can be made without the witness. Because I do not like having to respond to them in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please move on, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have one more point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, you were pointed to, I believe, the duty operations notebook if I'm using the correct terminology, and your name was mentioned. And you had indicated specifically that it was incorrect as far as how many men are arrived from which units. Do you recall that line of questioning from Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. The entries where it says the 2nd Battalion, 2-35, and then 35, saw there were figures there about the number of troops and who was supposed to be where.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And your testimony was that those figures to the best of your knowledge were incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figures were incorrect. That did not -- they did not correspond to the actual situation, to the troops who were with me and with Jevtic. They did not correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Which leads us to one of the conundrums. How is it that a duty operation officer would put down something on a note, a notebook, that is not totally accurate? Because later on, for instance, in the Tribunal, they may try to use that notebook to say these events occurred because they're written down?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty operations officer probably received that data from someone because he did not know the figures of troops. He probably received those figures from the chief. And as such, wrote them down. That would be the proper procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And can we conclude, then, that by looking at the duty operations notebook, one would have to go beyond just what is written down on paper to discern whether the events described in the notebook are true, accurate, and complete?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information itself, the one in the notebook, about the number of troops does not say much. It simply says what unit was with Maric, with me, and they needed the figures for logistics and for food and so on. Whereas for the events, the events are recorded as the information comes in from the field or from the commander. Orders coming in from him would be recorded, and then forwarded further on as well. So all that is recorded here are the figures. I don't know for what other purpose except for logistics they needed these figures. It is possible that figures are increased and do not correspond to the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To go back to my question concretely, and I'm speaking as a general principle, not with respect to that particular day, it would appear at least from what we've heard from you that one would have to go beyond what's written down on the paper and not merely rely on the notebook itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Rhetorical and already asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It wasn't quite answered, Your Honour, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think this question is quite obvious that of course what we are doing to verify what is said in those notebooks. So I believe in this sense there is no need to pursue in that direction at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Sometimes even the most obvious we need to nail down on the record. But if it's obvious and if it's on the record and if Mr. President and the Judges are satisfied, in that case, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, cross-examination, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Maric. I will go over some of these documents with you, and I will ask you about some areas that I have some concerns about as I just mentioned so you can respond to those concerns. Now, just on this last point, the duty officer notebook, that's a book that a commander may look into to help him determine what occurred while he was gone. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Commander could take a look at the notebook. It would also be sort of a reminder for the duty officer in case commander asked him about what was happening at such and such hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when the duty officer's doing a draft daily combat report, he may very well refer to these -- to this duty officer notebook to fill in those crucial details. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this notebook does not have a complete recitation of the events that occurred during any particular days, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. There is more a summary as such. Simply the events are recorded chronologically as they are taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, let's go to that notebook if we could. I believe it has been marked as P133. The English translation is now P133, I think A bis is what we have marked for the 12th because we didn't have that translation until this witness came. And if we could let that witness -- he might as well see what we believe is the original. And perhaps it would be -- if you could go to what is -- there should be a little red number which I'm sure you recognise is not part of the original. But it's 02935732. And that is page 2 of the July 12th notebook which is the time period that I believe you were duty officer. And I just want to go down to the section that I think you've already mentioned, the military police were sent for an ambush in Dzafin Kamen. But then I note that it says, "Eight buses from the Drina Trans and two of our buses from military police and four of our trucks are going to Bratunac today," did you write that down, what I said about the buses?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This entry says here, "Eight buses are going today, two of our buses from military police, and four of our trucks are going to Bratunac today, reported to the ministry in Zvornik." And I probably received this information from the chief of transportation service, and we can see on the left that chief of staff was at the 7th Battalion, and he probably received that information there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So you would have reported this information to Obrenovic who was at the 7th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And are these buses and trucks the ones that are in response to the Ministry of Defence order to send down for the Srebrenica evacuations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most likely, this was done pursuant to that telegram because I see that Ministry of Defence is mentioned here, that they were informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If I could go down, as it says that these trucks are going to Bratunac today. And then in the English, it says: "Reported to," but we can't read who it was reported to. Can you read it from the original?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reported to the Ministry of Defence in Zvornik. Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were just getting back to them on the original request. Okay. Then the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that a question or is that an answer from Mr. McCloskey? That's his interpretation. I understand it may be correct, and it probably is correct. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think this could be easily turned into a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was meant as a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were getting back to the Ministry of Defence on their original request?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. It was reported to the Ministry of Defence what vehicles were dispatched to Bratunac at their request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next section, there's a little star, and it says: "8th pb." Now, that's the 8th Infantry Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The 8th Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So at the time, was the 8th Infantry Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade attached to the Bratunac Brigade as the Bratunac 4th Infantry Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that it was outside the composition of the Zvornik Brigade. Radika Petrovic, the commander, was part of our brigade. And as far as I know, this was not transferred to the Bratunac Brigade, this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you, as it goes down at 1315 [sic] hours, "Bokcin Potok, there are blocked between three to four thousand Muslims. One was captured alive. And the Turks have four or five dead." Who did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information came through the information centre through the 8th Infantry Battalion just as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see that "Radika requested assistance and manpower to stop the Turks." Do you recall speaking directly to Radika, or was this just being passed on as it is sometimes done?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall whether I talked to Radika directly or whether the message was passed on through the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the Radika, Radika that is mentioned here, which Radika would that have been?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 8th Infantry Battalion, Radika Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to honour his request and provide him with any men or materials?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As the duty officer, I did not have this possibility. All I could do was pass on this information to the chief, Obrenovic, and then it is noted down that "We are sending the Praga, bring it in from Brezanci."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was a Praga as far as you know sent to help Radika in his area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the commander, I think, issued the order that the Praga should go towards the 8th Battalion, and I think it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And would that have been in the area of Kajici?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the area of Kajici, in the area covered by the 8th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not too far from Sandici on the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac Road?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where Sandici are located, but Konjevic Polje is quite far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Konjevic Polje is quite far from Kajici?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite a few kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just roughly. We may be just getting mixed up on what we think is quite far.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kajici is, I think, 7 or 8 kilometres or more from Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And that phone number, 881-529, and it says "Kajici," was that Radika's number as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, telephone numbers beginning 881 were in Kajici. This is a number, a PTT number, a number used by the normal telephone services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that could have been a house in Kajici? You don't remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Calls for speculation. It could have been a house. I think it should be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just asking him to search his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He's asking the gentleman to speculate. There's a big difference between searching memory and speculating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the witness did not give a very clear answer, not to the question posed by the Prosecution. The question was: "Was that Radika's number, so far as you remember?" It's a yes or no question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I don't have a problem with that. It was the house situation. That threw me off a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can just try to get to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this number written in the book Radika Petrovic's number?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here on the right-hand side in my handwriting, it says, "Give him Radika's phone number." Underneath is a phone number in Kajici. So most probably it's Radika's phone number at his command post in Kajici. But it's a PTT number. Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So you were receiving information about what was going on down in that area, including three to four thousand Muslims. Did you report that information to the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did transmit this information to the chief of staff, and we can see on the following page that he issued specific orders to certain organs and units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And now if we could, I'd like to go to a daily combat report. It's dated 12 July. It's P450. I think we have a B/C/S version. I just want to ask you briefly about it. You can scan over it, and you may want to look at the end, too, because there's some initials there, MM and SS. I'm just going to ask you about a couple of things, so if you need to read it after my questions, please let me know. But I don't need you to study the whole thing right now, but if you feel you need to, that's fine. Just looking at the initials, is this something that you drafted as the duty officer that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. MM, that's probably my initials. As for SS, I can't recall now who typed this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then looking at the front page under point 2, it does confirm there that "We sent one Praga with crew to the area of the 8th Battalion in Kajici." And you wrote in that information, I take it, based on what you'd learned as duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here, yes. It says here, "This information was passed on," and we did send off a Praga crew to the area of the 8th pb in Kajici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know what it says, but I'm just trying to refresh your recollection because it's your testimony that is also equally as important. So my next question would be: Do you know when that Praga came back to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know because I wasn't at the command any longer. I went out on to the ground the next day, so I don't know when it came back and where it went afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you left the duty officer position, I think you said about 9.00 on the 13th, you hadn't received any information that that Praga had come back. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I think there is either a mistake here or a misinterpretation or a wrong translation. We heard that Mr. McCloskey said that he left his duty operations post on the 13th in the evening. It was not in the evening; it was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: From the transcript, we see it's in the morning, 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I meant to say in the morning at 9.00. So had you heard any news about this Praga before you left your duty officer job?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't receive any information, nor do I know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just a little bit below that part about the Praga, well, again, we see the eight buses and the two buses from the military police. So those were actually two buses from the Zvornik Brigade military police that were sent to Bratunac. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information, observation, eight buses, two buses, four trucks, the telegram asked for all available vehicles. And what is noted down here is what was dispatched pursuant to that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that. But in direct examination, I seem to recall you not being clear whether the buses were -- whether or not the Zvornik Brigade had buses. And it appears from this document that these are Zvornik Brigade military police buses. So that's why I asked you. Are these Zvornik Brigade military police buses?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade did have a few buses, but they were mostly out of order. We can see from this that at that point we had two buses in good working order, and we did dispatch those two. I think we had four or five buses all together, but what you can see here is that we dispatched two. The police did not have any buses, so it can only be our military post, VP, in other words, can only refer to our military post. It cannot refer to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for clearing that up. Okay, the next line says: "One military police detachment was sent to Konjevic Polje pursuant to your order." Now, you wrote this. Can you tell us more about it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to this testimony and what I said in Banja Luka to the investigators, I do not remember this telegram. I don't recall it. I don't recall that I noted this down while I was on duty. There's no reason for me not to believe that it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Having -- I don't think this was shown to you in your interview. Perhaps it was. But having read it now, does that refresh your recollection as to what this is about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I received an order about instructions from the military police at anybody's request, and I don't remember any activities taking place pursuant to this. However, when I look at it now, if such an order had arrived, I would most probably have noted it down according to someone's order to Konjevic Polje. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you heard after the fact about anybody being killed in Konjevic Polje around the 12th and 13th?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically about the murders, I heard about that. There was talk about it. But I learned about it from the media and from the Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you didn't hear about any murders in -- after the fall of Srebrenica, only from the media and at the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received official, reliable information when I followed the Krstic trial. That's when I learned that the events had taken the course they did and that there were executions. Before that, people said there had been fighting on the road to Konjevic Polje and up there. But it was from the trial that I learned the real truth and what events actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Just one last point on this: It says "pursuant to your order." Now, this is a document going out under the signature or the name -- not the signature but the name at this point of Vinko Pandurevic. What is the reference to "your order"? Is that an order from the -- Can you tell us who the "your" would be in this reference? Who would have given the order according to this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was probably issued by the command of the Drina Corps because it is to them that this telegram is addressed. So this was carried out pursuant to their order. The signatory is Vinko Pandurevic who is officially the commander regardless of the fact that he's not in the field, someone is acting for him. It's the chief of staff. So he was the one who signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, are there regular wire connections between the comms room of the standard headquarters and the battalions of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the battalions, that is, the Zvornik Brigade, had wire connections with all subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we've heard about an operations centre which was on a hill above Zvornik. Was there a wire connection between the Zvornik headquarters at Standard and this operations centre up on the hill?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The operations centre was linked with the operations duty officer who could receive all information and pass it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: By wire, like the battalions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations centre was in the building of the Zvornik Brigade, one floor up from the duty room. And it had all the wire connections with all the subordinates. On a nearby hill across the asphalt road, there was a radio centre which had radio links. This could not be done from the first building, so we had links with the comms room which had wire links. The radio centre did not have wire connections, but only radio connections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm talking about the radio place on the hill above Zvornik. Did that have a wire connection to the Zvornik Brigade like all the battalions did?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it did. Because it wouldn't have been a problem to establish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in speaking over the wire, there's no way to intercept that over the airwaves, is there? You can only intercept a wire by tapping into it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, for my belated objection, but no foundation has been laid as to whether this gentleman would know that information. So I think some predicate questions are required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, It's a technical question. I'm afraid this witness is capable to answer this question or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, was that a difficult question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, it doesn't go the complexity of the question. It goes to the knowledge of the individual. He can lay some questions such as whether he has any technical knowledge with respect to wire, radio communications and so on and so forth. Perhaps he may be able to answer that question. He may have some other information that we don't know. If he wants to ask a general question, that's fine. But the way it's phrased, I'm afraid it's going beyond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think these technical questions, some people are able to answer it, some not. We just need the answer from this witness whether he's capable to answer this question or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That would be...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you may answer that question if you could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, tapping into the wire connections, this is a closed system. And it didn't happen. It did happen that the wires would be cut off in the fighting, and that for protracted periods of time there would be no connection, and then the signalsman had to go out and search for the place where the line had been cut off. But as far as I know, there was no wiretapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So if Zvornik headquarters was going to communicate with the radio centre on the hill, their communications would be private if done over the wire communication? They would not be able to be intercepted by anybody?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, it calls --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is just pure harassment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm Your Honour, I'm not trying -- I'm trying to assist the gentleman. Because this gentleman here, the witness, is not a technician. No foundation has been laid, you know. If he wants to ask the right questions, fine, and establish him as an expert or perhaps have some specific knowledge, I have no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Your Honour, if I may, they brought in a gazillion number of these wire experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this point. He's just making a circus of Mr. Stojanovic's case like he did his own, and it's just ridiculous. And I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, first of all, this witness testified he studied engineering. Secondly, this question is just a logical follow up from the answers given by this witness previously. So we see no problem at all for the Prosecution to put this question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have some major objections with that, Your Honour. But very well. And I would appreciate it if Mr. McCloskey would exercise some self-control. Some of his comments are unprofessional and degrading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope both of you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have been, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- could do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Don't stand up so quickly. Yes. Maybe you could repeat your question, Mr. McCloskey, to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So as a duty officer, you're going to be concerned about whether or not your communications could be intercepted, I would take it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. On my telephone, it said, "Caution, the enemy is listening in." So we had to take account of the security of our communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you're speaking to the radio centre on the hill above Zvornik on the wire, the enemy can't listen in to that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly with the duty operations officer through the wire connection. But our comms room in the building, and the radio centre, had both wire communications and radio communications. And then the conversations could be listened into.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Conversations over the radio could be listened into if nonencrypted, I take it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And hardwire connections cannot be. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless they are wiretapped, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you as duty officer or as commander wanted to speak to the radio centre on the hill about important material, you would go on the hardwire, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communication went through our comms room would establish communication with the radio centre. What means they used, most often it was the way you've described. But we cannot exclude the possibility that they communicated by radio. The centre could communicate with the radio centre both by radio and by wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, the radio centre would want to communicate the way the commander told them to, wouldn't they? They're not on their own going to spread open information over the airwaves in a combat situation. They would know better than that at the radio centre, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. They would stick to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A speaker speaking over -- speaking from the duty office or speaking from the comms room at the brigade could tell whether they were speaking over a hardwire or over a radio. Correct? I think you're the one that talked about this earlier.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could tell. You could usually tell by the actual conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go to Exhibit P121. These are what you've looked at before they are what has been referred to as tactical intercepts that the Muslims, the local Muslims were -- some information they were able to get from listening to the airwaves. And I want to direct you to what is under their notes, under the 13th of July. It's page 3 in the English translation. And it should be -- referring to the B/C/S version, if you could just look at it where it begins on the 13th and just the first several lines, there's just talk about some basic information. Do you see where it starts "13 July" and then it starts off at "164.050, there was one dead"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that "participant 188 asked Omega" and so on...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Those first few lines I'm not really asking you about, but if you could just keep following, it talks about, "They allowed only military MUP and military police to pass over Crni Vrh because the escort was required for the others." You had talked about there being a roadblock on that road near Crni Vrh on the 13th in the evening when you went there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They sent reinforcements towards Josanica. He that is that road over Crni Vrh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then the intercept operators talk about: "On RU 12, frequency 238 was active because of the Lovcen net, the users of the same RMR are," and then it describes various users, "Igman, Igman 1 personally, Lovac 1, Pekos," and it goes on. I believe you testified on direct that Lovac 1 was Dragan Obrenovic, the chief of staff at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Lovac 1 was Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: According to these intercepts, Lovac 1 was active on the radio with these other units in the area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are all participants in the radio net.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So where would he have been if he's active on the radio? What are the options? If he can be picked up by these Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to ask -- this is beyond the scope of this gentleman's knowledge. I just want to register my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your objection is registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This clearly would be on a radio, correct? Not a hard line.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. These are the participants in the radio net, and these are the intercepted radio signals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At this time in the evening on the 13th, you know that there's an emergency situation in your area. You're trying to gather troops together. Troops are being deployed. It would be a natural place for Obrenovic to be at the time, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were only a few men there. Maybe there were about 50 to 55 of us. We were to deploy. I didn't see him up there the entire time until the next day in the morning, just like I said in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that. But listen to my question. It would have been a natural place for the commander to be at the time, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander probably in his view had other places where he thought he should have been, rather than the one where we were. Perhaps he was in that sector. But he was not at the positions where this particular unit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So perhaps he was in the Snagovo area, but he wasn't just in -- where you could see him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that he was at Kula, Maricici, Snagovo. These are all the places he could have maintained radio communications and could have been a participant in the radio net.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we look down the page a little more, we see: "Amazon 1 to Lovac: Tell Vuk to call. The chief is on his way towards you and Vuk went past Amazon towards the base." So if the chief is Obrenovic, we can tell minimally from this that he's on the way towards somewhere. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. You could see from this message that he was moving, that he was somewhere on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it goes at 2050 hours: "Lovac 1 reported to Lovac that a column was moving below Zlatni Kamen." You've testified earlier that Lovac is this radio centre on the hill. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if this is correct, Obrenovic can't be on the radio from the radio centre on the top of the hill. He's in the field somewhere reporting to the top of the hill?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this information at 2050 hours, Lovac, Obrenovic, informed the station that the column was moving below Zlatni Kamen. I don't know if he received the information from Vukotic or if he saw that for himself. That, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know who Celik was, whose code name was Celik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we know, and you have testified about the 14th of July. Did you have a radio man with you when you were in the field on the 13th and 14th July?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I came up there to the 4th unit, it had its own communications, and the communication officer who was together with Jevtic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that Jevtic, you received information that Jevtic really wasn't able to handle the responsibility of command at this time, at this crucial point on the 13th of July. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he sent me up there, Obrenovic told me that -- he informed me about the composition, said that Jevtic was the commander. But in view of the composition, the way it was, Jevtic will probably not be able to carry this out in a good way, that the soldiers would probably not listen to him. So that is probably why he was sent to that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And Jevtic was a guy that, like many others, got drafted at the beginning of the war, and he by profession was a civil engineer, not a military man. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. He was a reserve officer. He had a rank. He had spent quite some time in the war. But just as you said, his duty were mostly engineering ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was a lieutenant at the time, July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that he was a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were a major? Or were you a captain?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at the time I was still a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know that Jevtic had just been appointed to be the commander of the engineering company, I believe, in April or May of that year?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when he was appointed to that duty. But I know that at the time he was at the post of commander of the engineering company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So when Dragan Obrenovic sent you to the area, were you sent to take command of those units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As an operations officer, I went out to the field, into the field many times. I also held the post of a company commander. I was the head of a tactical company. And I would get the official order that I was the commander that this unit was being sent to such and such a place. In this case, there was no such official order. I was just asked by Obrenovic to go and help to organise that unit, in order to take up positions of some sort up there and also to meet the men who would be arriving that night and the next day. This is how I understood it, and this is exactly how I implemented it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you designated by Obrenovic to take command of Jevtic's unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He did not designate me as the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your job?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job was to coordinate the unit up there which was made up from different units, and to make sure that the task that Jevtic was given is implemented, to set up some kind of defence, and to meet the men who were arriving and to link them all up. As you yourself said, Jevtic had military experience in combat operations. And I had also been through a lot. So I used my knowledge to implement the task and to preserve the lives of the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That would have been in direct contradiction to the principle of unity of command, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sometimes it would happen that there would be a command, but then sometimes somebody would send from the superior command to help this commander in the implementation of a task so that that person would be working according to the instructions of the person who had arrived; in this case, specifically, they would work or he would work in accordance with my instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The commander of that unit that night would have been responsible for the care and the custody of any prisoners taken, wouldn't he, including their murders if they were murdered by people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. No one was captured that night. There were people captured in the morning. These prisoners were treated professionally and correctly. There were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're aware Dragan Obrenovic stated that he put you in command that night?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was in Banja Luka with the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, I read his statement. The investigator asked me if I agreed with that statement, and I told him, just as I am telling you now, that I did not agree, that this was not the way it was. He did not designate me as the commander of that unit, and that I was not the commander of the unit. They asked me whether I was the highest-ranking officer there when I arrived, and I was. But the next day, I was not. The next day, there were also majors there. But they were also not in the function of the commanders of that unit. Each unit had its own commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have maybe I hope not more than 10 or 15 more minutes. But I see it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let me consult with our Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, any redirect, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I noted down two questions, but in view of the requirement and the need of this witness to travel tomorrow because of his work obligations, I don't think that this would be so critical. So I would grant the time to Mr. McCloskey. I think that we will finish what we need to do in under a minute because we just need to tender one exhibit, and that is the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So far, I might have one question, maybe two. But I don't know. I don't know what the next 15 minutes will bear. So... I can't read into Mr. McCloskey's mind, nor has he shared with me his outline. But so far, he's okay. He's doing okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. We'll continue to sit for another 15 minutes and try to finish this witness today. And I apologise for the interpreters and the court reporters about this delay. I wonder whether we could be allowed to continue by the interpreters and the court reporters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will continue for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. I appreciate your cooperation. Mr. McCloskey, try to make your cross-examination as concise as possible so that we could make the best use of the time available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, going back to the 14th of July, were you able to hear radio traffic over the radio at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did have communications up and running at the time. I could talk, and I could listen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, according to the Muslims, they heard this exchange, and according to Dragan Obrenovic, he heard over his radio the same exchange on the 14th of July. And it's something you discussed already. "For Maric, Miladinovic, Mitrovic, engineers, to come at Nedjo's inn with the excavator in order to widen a road. They went to Sava 66." Did you hear that over the radio like Obrenovic said he did, and the Muslims obviously did?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I read this information. I read that later and when I was

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: and I don't know if Jevtic received that message because Jevtic also had a communications person who was with him. The message did not reach me.

utterances.speaker: THE HAGUE INVESTIGATORS
utterances.text: Well, what is -- has been established was that, and I think you've said yourself, Dragan Obrenovic came to the scene there in this area, and in fact Miladinovic and Mitrovic were ordered and did leave, as you yourself saw. So my question is: Were you also ordered to go to Nedjo's inn at the time like it says in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody ordered me to go to Nedjina Kafana, to that inn the day after -- actually, the following day, two days had gone by.

utterances.speaker: THE HAGUE INVESTIGATORS
utterances.text: All right. And do you recall telling the investigators when you interviewed in Banja Luka that you had heard Obrenovic on the radio during the day on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was in command when the operations began. He was with us until we began to spread out. Then I went to the right flank. I didn't physically see him. But later when the combat operations started, when we clashed with the enemy, I heard him over the radio, over the radio connection.
