And then when I actually came to the Snagovo Road, he was already there.

utterances.speaker: THE HAGUE INVESTIGATORS
utterances.text: What time was this when you saw him at the Snagovo Road on the 14th roughly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pullout lasted until about 2200 or 2300 hours. He was up there. We waited until all of the soldiers pulled out so that we could see what the situation was in terms of the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE HAGUE INVESTIGATORS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me see if this refreshes your recollection. Well, of course you've already testified the morning of the 14th you saw him in the Snagovo area. In fact, he interrogated some of those prisoners. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he questioned them. He interrogated them. After that was finished, he waited for Zoran to come, and then he ordered what he ordered. He interrogated them, and then he made a fast decision, and that is what he decided.

utterances.speaker: THE HAGUE INVESTIGATORS
utterances.text: Okay. And in talking about that, you say: "He stayed there at the intersection of the road where, as I had to prepare the line for combat, I went towards the location of Jasekovici. And after this deployment of troops and getting ready for combat and everything else, the next time that I saw him on that day was sometime just before dark at 8.00 in the evening about 2000 hours, moves, and I heard him issuing orders and commanding between 1600 and 1800 hours over the radio." So you say you see him in the morning of the 14th, and then you say you actually see him just before dark at about 8.00, but that you hear him over the radio from 4 -- well, 1600 to 1800 hours. Is that correct what you told the folks in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told them as well roughly, as far as the timing is concerned. I cannot exactly recall what time it was. It was approximately in the afternoon before it got dark. But it's very hard for a person to remember after such a long time, whether this was at 4.00 p.m. or at 6.00 p.m. I know that immediately prior to the clash with the Muslim forces, I could hear him over the radio. He commanded throughout the entire operation during the pullout, and then when the truce went into force, so he was constantly on the radio. Once I got to the road, physically reached the road, I saw him there. He was in a vehicle. By that time, it was already dark. When the pullout was completed, it was already dark. So it was probably quite late. It was the month of July.

utterances.speaker: THE HAGUE INVESTIGATORS
utterances.text: Okay. And you also told the people in Banja Luka that he had his jeep with him, and a driver, but you said it was pretty risky to drive anywhere. Was that correct, it was pretty risky to be driving around?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a jeep there. And his driver, I remember that I was wet. I changed my clothes, and I put all of my clothing in my backpack. I put it in the jeep, and then that jeep disappeared. Later, as I heard from the driver, I heard that the Muslims transferred it to Nezuk.

utterances.speaker: THE HAGUE INVESTIGATORS
utterances.text: Okay. And then the investigator asked you: "And on the 14th when you saw him at his jeep, how long did you remain with him for?" And you say: "Basically, we were trying to regroup the troops after the clashes with the enemy. This operation of regrouping lasted until 1.00 at night. And he was there." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately. I'm not sure whether it was about 2300 hours or 0100 hours. I don't know. I cannot tell you exactly until what time this was. The pullout lasted until about 2300 hours. We could see what the situation was, what the head count was. But I don't think that the whole thing went on longer than 1.00 a.m. He was with this jeep. And later, then I didn't see him. I only saw him then the next day -- next morning.

utterances.speaker: THE HAGUE INVESTIGATORS
utterances.text: The question is: "And this takes us to 1.00 a.m. On the 15th." And you say: "Yes. And at that time, it had started to rain, and the troops regrouped and waiting for the daybreak." And the question was: "Was Obrenovic with you from 1.00 a.m. hours on?" And you say: "I saw his vehicle, I know that his vehicle was there, and I know that he was there. And it's a rather big stretch of the area where the troops were deployed. It was maybe 4 to 5 kilometres. So he might have been doing some rounds or going to inspect the troops or something, but I remember having seen him at the crack of dawn at that morning. Well, given the fact that you could virtually hear the Muslim forces going by, I don't suppose he could have gone anywhere. We had to remain there because -- which I think is corroborated by the fact that I saw him at daybreak. We were all there together." So you say, "We were all there together" and that you saw his vehicle there. Does this -- do you have any corrections or comments on what you told the Banja Luka folks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's mostly what it is. I think that one just needs to read that carefully. He was there with a vehicle. He was moving around. I said all of us were there. And that means that he might have been there, too. I cannot claim with certainty whether he was in the vehicle or not. But let me tell you that it was crazy to attempt to leave that place and go anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: THE HAGUE INVESTIGATORS
utterances.text: Okay. And in your direct examination, you were asked about when you were alone with Dragan Jokic talking to him about these events. And you said: "Yes, on several occasions, I asked Jokic whether he knew about those events, especially after the information that came to light during the Krstic trial which we learned through the media. I asked him whether he knew anything about this, whether he had taken part in it and so on. I never got a reply to the effect that he had participated or known about anything that was going on at the time." Okay, now I want to read to you what you told the investigators in Banja Luka on this same topic. Have you had a chance to review your interview from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE HAGUE INVESTIGATORS
utterances.text: Mr. Manning says: "Explain to me what you mean by `cover things up.' What intention anyone made to cover things up that you know of." And you say: "Later on I found that they were trying to cover up the executions, and then they were trying to cover up the graves and the graves were relocated, secondary graves. And there was a very narrow circle of people who knew about these activities." And Mr. Manning asked you again: "Do you know who that narrow circle was?" And you say this: "Commander, chief of staff, security, intelligence, police. I think also the engineering. I worked with Jokic in the same office, and that's been going on for two years. And whenever I ask him what happened, I never received any answers." Very similar to what you testified in Court, but in Banja Luka you concluded that that engineering was part of the inner circle involved in this, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we could object to lack of clarity. You know that the engineering corps, the 5th Battalion and the engineering unit of the Zvornik Brigade have not been defined properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that the witness could answer that question, if he needs some explanation on that. Witness, please answer that question if you could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've said in the statement, I can repeat that later, which means later when I learned from the media about what transpired in Krstic trial, I learned of things that I had no idea had happened. So when I mentioned the engineering unit, what I meant to say was that that entire effort could not have been completed without the use of the engineering units which were involved in various tasks, including sanitisation of the terrain and so on. And as for the narrow circle of people, many senior officers from the command could confirm to you that they had no ideas that something like this could have happened in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE HAGUE INVESTIGATORS
utterances.text: So you stand by what you said to the investigators in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I stated, and that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Your Honours, stemming from the previous questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maric, the forward command post, did it have wire connections with the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that forward command post did not have hard wire connections. To tell you the truth, I never was present there. I mean, I wasn't on duty there, but I think that they did not have hardwire connections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Forward command posts, did they have radio communication with the battalions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had radio connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And from the forward command post, was it possible to command the battalions in extraordinary circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was ordered by the commander in certain circumstances when that order extended to the forward command post as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I want to go back to the issue of the Praga, and you were shown a daily report, and also you had the logbook. And in the log -- the daily report you indicate, and I quote, "We sent one Praga." And then it goes on. My question is, do you know for a fact whether the Praga was sent, or was that a conclusion that you made based on the information that you had from the logbook?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information came from the logbook. I personally didn't see the Praga. I don't know what it was sent, for what purpose. All I know is what is recorded in the logbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, do you know if it was actually sent? That's the whole question? I know it's in the logbook, and I know it's in the daily report. But the question is: Do you know for a fact whether it was sent because a series of questions were asked about when it came back. So do you know for a fact if it was sent? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim with certainty, but based on what I recorded, it is most probable that it had been sent because I probably wouldn't have recorded something that wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you take that analogy, then what was recorded by somebody else in a logbook about how many men were sent to you, then that also would have to be correct, would it not? But you told us that was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I know that. I don't think there's a good logic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I don't mean to impeach the gentleman. But very well. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any documents to tender? Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. We hereby tender D132/3, which is a topographic map used by the witness during examination-in-chief. The rest of the documents are already in evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. On your part, do you have any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just the English translation of the 12 July notebook bring, P133/a bis. The B/C/S has been in the record. But now we have the English to correspond to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think during that time, the Bench asked for the translations already, so there should be no problem if the B/C/S is admitted into evidence. So it is admitted into evidence as well as D132/3 the map, is admitted into evidence. Thank you, Witness, for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. And when this Court is adjourned, the usher will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home. At this point, I have to say that we are very much grateful to the cooperation of the interpreters and the court reporter. We are about 26 minutes past the time, and I'm not going to talk about the examinations at this time. But maybe we could find another way to make up the time we used for them, for instance, by breaking earlier sometime. But anyway, we are very grateful, and I appreciate their cooperation. The hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of July, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 25
